segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So for -ar verbs we have -é for I—hablar, to speak; hablé, I spoke—and -ó for he, she, it, you formal, and we're accenting our endings:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: hablé, habló.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For -er / -ir verbs we have an "ee" sound, so an "i", an -í, for I, and -ió, -i-o, for he, she, it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have -í and -ió.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you go to comer, to eat, "I ate" is comí, and "he ate, she ate, it ate, you formal ate" is comió.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We're accenting the endings again: the -í and the -ó. Comí, comió.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comí, comió.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. What was salir? Salir.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: To leave.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To leave, or to go out. So how would you say, "I went out," or "I left"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Salí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salí. "She went out," "she left"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Salió.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salió. Good. "She didn't go out yet." "She didn't leave yet."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No salió todavía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No salió todavía. "I don't know why she didn't leave yet." "I don't know why she didn't leave yet."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No sé por qué no salió todavía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No sé por qué no salió todavía. What did que mean? Que, what does that mean?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: What.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, what. And what else does it mean?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: That.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That, in like "I hope that", espero que. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So apart from "what" and "that", que also means "than", than, so you can use it like this.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you could say, for example, "I ate more than him." "I ate", it's the first bit.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comé...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: -er / -ir verb.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "I ate more than him."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comí más que él.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Not "him", than "he", more than he ate.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comí más que él. "I ate more than him" or "more than he" ate.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "He ate more than me."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comió más que... and I'm not sure if it's me or mijo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: When we said comí más que él, we put él there because whilst in English we say "him", what we really mean is "he"—"I ate more than he ate".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's quite peculiar in English that we say "him" and not "he".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in Spanish we're being more literal: comí más que él, "I ate more than he". So "he ate more than me", comió más que...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. So he ate more than I, he ate more than I ate. So how would that be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comió más que yo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Comió más que yo. It's actually quite peculiar in English that we say "me". In fact, the way we use words like "me" instead of "I" is very peculiar in English,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and it's a negative language transfer that could influence other languages that you're learning. For example, if I say, "Who wants to go to the park?" you might say, "Me!"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This doesn't make any sense. It's "I! I want to go to the park." Where's this "me"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So there is some strange use of these words in English that might influence our Spanish, so we need to cut that negative language transfer when we identify it popping up.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, comió más que yo, "he ate more than I", he ate more than I ate.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "to see"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ver.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ver. Good. "I saw"—ver is regular here, huh? So "I saw"—

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So go back to comer, use that as your hook.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vi.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "I saw him"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo vi.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo vi. "I didn't see him"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No lo vi.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No lo vi. "I saw him, but he didn't see me." And as we're contrasting, we will probably use one or both of the words for "I" and "he", those words we don't need to use. We will probably use one or both of them here as we're contrasting, although you don't need to,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: so it's up to you. "I saw him, but he didn't see me." First bit is "I saw him".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo vi.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "But he didn't see me."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pero no me vio.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo vi pero no me vio.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And like I said, as we're contrasting, we might feel an urge to say the word for él—lo vi pero él no me vio, or yo lo vi pero él no me vio. Depends on the context. Even if you have context and you know who you're talking about, you might feel yourself wanting to say these words because you're contrasting.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for "nothing", nothing, in Spanish is nada. Nada.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: N-a-d-a, nada.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And we have double negative in Spanish, which means you can say, "I didn't see nothing."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No vi nada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No vi nada. "I didn't eat anything."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No comí nada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No comí nada. "Didn't you eat anything?" speaking formally. "Didn't you eat anything?"

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿No comió nada?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿No comió nada? "Why didn't you eat anything?"

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Por qué no comió nada?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Por qué no comió nada? Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for "nobody" is nadie.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nadie.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: N-a-d-i-e, nadie.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nadie.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Nobody saw anything." "Nobody saw nothing."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nadie vio nada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nadie vio nada. Good. Nobody saw anything.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Durar, durar, means to last. Durar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Durar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We have endure in English...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Duration.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Duration. And you even get like corporate names that use these Latin roots and kind of appeal to your understanding without you realizing that you understand it. So, for example, you have Duracell batteries. You know what that means, but you don't know why you know what it means. So you can identify this kind of use of Latin in industry and how it's appealing to your subconscious understanding of the message that they want to give you about the products. So look out for that.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So durar, to last. "Minute" in Spanish is minuto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say, "It lasted two minutes"? "It lasted two minutes."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Duró dos minutos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Duró dos minutos. "I lasted two minutes"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Duré dos minutos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Duré dos minutos. We looked at before how you can get this "-ing" adjective. So the adjective that we have for "-ing" like "interesting", using -ante or -iente. So "interesting" was interesante. So "during" is not an adjective, but it's formed in the same way. So how do you think you say "during" in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Durante.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Durante. So you could say, "during two minutes"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Durante dos minutos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And you can use that like "for" as well. So we said that with time you can say por dos minutos, but you can also say durante, you will hear that as well in Spanish: durante dos minutos, "during two minutes", "for two minutes".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "to eat"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comer. Good. And "he ate"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comió.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comió. How would you say, "He ate for half an hour," or "He ate during half an hour"? "Half an hour" is media, half, and what was "hour"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hora.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hora, like in ahora. Media hora. Good. So, "He ate during half an hour." "He ate for half an hour."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comió durante media hora.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Comió durante media hora. "He spoke during half an hour," "for half an hour"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habló durante media hora.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Habló durante media hora.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "with" in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Con.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Con. "Without" in Spanish is sin, s-i-n, sin.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sin.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sin. And "to stop", to stop, is parar. Parar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: P-a-r-a-r, parar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Parar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you could say, "He spoke for half an hour without stopping." "He spoke for half an hour without stopping."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habló durante media hora sin parar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Habló durante media hora sin parar. And we said that after prepositions, so sin is a preposition, we're not saying "stopping", we're saying "to stop". Sin parar, without to stop. Habló durante media hora sin parar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Parar is interesting, because par, par in Spanish means pair. So un par is a pair, so like a pair of shoes: un par de zapatos, un par de zapatos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So parar, to stop, might be "the pairing". You can imagine this kind of time and space notion of of two things pairing, reaching each other, and then stopping.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And then comparar, to compare, is "with pairing".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So even though this is an "m" here, it's con, the the "n" has been softened by that "p", which is why we say compare. So with pairing is to compare.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Prepare, of course, is pre-pairing. We can see this in English as well, no?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Repair, to repair is to re-pair, to pair up again.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Separar is to separate in Spanish: separation, separación; separar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And this se- means apart. So to separate is to pair apart, to pair apart.
